strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question — whether thinking models acquire new reasoning capabilities or repurpose pre-existing ones — with a creative hybrid-model experimental design that combines base-model generation with thinking-model-guided steering.

The unsupervised SAE-based taxonomy construction across five thinking models (varying architecture and scale, including both distilled and RLVR-trained models) is a thoughtful attempt to avoid top-down annotation bias, and the grid search over layers/cluster sizes is systematic.
The ablation studies (Only-bias, Random-firing, Random-vectors) are the right controls to include and probe the mechanism.

Strong reproducibility posture: public codebase, one-command reproduction scripts, detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and honest disclosure of the narrower-default results (Tables 4–5) and of the LLM-as-judge validation gap.
Multiple base/thinking model pairs and two benchmarks give some breadth to the empirical evaluation.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is significantly confounded by the design of the hybrid model: the thinking model is in the loop at inference time in multiple ways (SAE classifier over the rollout, steering vectors trained on thinking-model completions, and — most importantly — selection of the steered token by lowest perplexity according to the thinking model, plus a coefficient/window sweep). The hybrid is effectively an ensemble where the thinking model scores candidate continuations, so the reported 91% gap recovery cannot be cleanly attributed to 'latent reasoning mechanisms in the base model'. A key missing control is thinking-model perplexity-based selection without steering (or a guided-decoding/ensemble baseline using the thinking model alone), which would isolate how much is attributable to the base model's latent capabilities versus the thinking model acting as a critic.

The paper's own ablation undercuts the headline 'when vs. how' framing: in the strongest setting, Only-bias reaches 76.8% vs. base 63.4%, meaning a generic bias vector alone recovers roughly 58% of the gap, while category-specific, correctly-timed steering vectors add only ~7.6 points (≈33% of the gap). Random-firing (77.8%) and Random-vectors (77.2%) perform comparably to Only-bias. Thus most of the improvement appears to come from style/format distillation via the bias vector, not from activating specific reasoning mechanisms at the right time — yet the abstract and conclusion present the opposite emphasis.

Test-set hyperparameter tuning: main-table results for smaller models are computed with a large sweep over coefficients {0.1–1.0} and token windows {0, −1, −15, −50, −100} apparently selected on the evaluation benchmarks. The appendix shows results collapse without the sweep (0.0% gap recovery for several pairs), so headline numbers (e.g., 'up to 91%') reflect heavy per-benchmark tuning rather than a robust effect, and no held-out validation protocol is described.

Results are highly heterogeneous and fragile: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B shows 0.0% gap recovery on both benchmarks, Llama-3.1-8B only 3.5% on MATH500, and GSM8K gap recovery for the 1.5B pair is negative (hybrid below base). The strong claims rest essentially on the 32B settings; the paper should temper its general conclusions accordingly.

No statistical treatment: single-run accuracies with differences as small as 1–2 points (e.g., 94.4% vs. 94.8% on GSM8K) are interpreted without confidence intervals or significance tests, on benchmarks of 500–1319 problems.

The 'unsupervised' taxonomy claim is weaker than advertised: category titles/descriptions are generated by o4-mini, and all three evaluation metrics (consistency, completeness, independence) are LLM-as-judge scores that the authors admit are unvalidated against human judgment; hyperparameter selection therefore optimizes an unvalidated LLM-judge proxy.

Presentation inconsistencies: the abstract states steering of '12% of tokens' while Table 3 reports up to 21.5%; the claim of 'no prior work' on steering reasoning in base models is somewhat strong given Venhoff et al. (2025), Ward et al. (2025), and concurrent work (Bogdan et al., 2025).

strengths: The central research question is important and well-motivated: whether RLVR/post-training teaches new reasoning capabilities or merely the timing of deployment of pre-existing capabilities is a significant open question for efficient training of reasoning models.

The paper covers an unusually broad set of base/thinking model pairs (five model configurations across Llama and Qwen architectures, both distilled and RLVR-trained thinking models) and two benchmarks, which is more extensive than much of the related interpretability work.

The ablation studies (Only-bias, Random-firing, Random-vectors) are well-designed and show that specific, correctly-timed steering vectors outperform generic baselines, supporting the paper's mechanism claim within its own setting.

The paper is transparent about weaknesses: it acknowledges that LLM-as-judge metrics are unvalidated against human judgment, and Appendix C.3/Tables 4-5 honestly report that results collapse without the full hyperparameter sweep.
A reproducibility statement with a public codebase, complete prompts, and full taxonomy tables in the appendix supports verification and follow-up work.
weaknesses: The hybrid setup does not cleanly support the headline claim. The 'hybrid model' is not the base model plus steering alone: at every step the thinking model (a) provides the SAE-based category signal for timing and (b) selects the final steered token by lowest perplexity under the thinking model. The generation is therefore continuously supervised by the thinking model's distribution, which directly confounds the claim that base models already possess the capabilities; the system plausibly succeeds largely because the thinking model is shepherding it.

Results are weak and cherry-picked in presentation. The headline 'recovers up to 91% of the gap' comes from the single best configuration; Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B shows 0% (actually negative) gap recovery on GSM8K, and Llama-3.1-8B only 3.5% on MATH500. Two of five configurations effectively fail, which materially weakens the generalization claim, yet the abstract and conclusion emphasize only the best case.

There is evidence of test-set hyperparameter tuning. The full sweep (coefficients {0.1,...,1.0} and token windows {0,-1,-15,-50,-100}) used for the main results selects steering settings by benchmark accuracy on the evaluation sets. The appendix tables show that without this sweep many results are negative (e.g., -8.4%, -5.4%, -1.2%). The headline numbers thus partly reflect evaluation-set optimization rather than a robust method; no held-out validation split is described.

The taxonomy evaluation is largely circular. Category titles/descriptions are generated by one LLM (o4-mini), and then consistency, completeness, and independence are all scored by LLMs (GPT-4.1-mini). The paper concedes alignment with human judgment is unvalidated, so the claimed 'interpretability, completeness, and independence' of the taxonomy, and the grid search in Figure 2 built on these scores, lack a validated ground truth.

The 'unsupervised, assumption-free' framing is overstated. SAEs with a tiny latent dimension, an assumed top-3 sparsity, the choice of sentence granularity, the layer/cluster-size grid, and LLM-driven category naming all impose substantial design assumptions; the authors themselves note that manually designed taxonomies 'would likely work similarly,' undermining the claimed methodological advantage over prior annotation-based work.

Only GSM8K and MATH500 are used to support strong general claims about reasoning mechanisms. Both are math benchmarks; no accuracy is accompanied by confidence intervals or significance tests, so differences such as +2.2% vs +1.8% (used to compute 'gap recovery' figures like 81.8% vs 57.9%) may not be statistically meaningful.

The taxonomy contribution (Section 2) is disconnected from the causal claim in ways that limit its value: the steering vector layer (37% depth) deliberately differs from the taxonomy-evaluation layer, and the results depend only on 'the existence of reasoning categories rather than their specific derivation method,' per the authors' own statement.

Novelty is incremental relative to closely related concurrent work (Venhoff et al. 2025, Ward et al. 2025, Galichin et al. 2025, Zhao et al. 2025) that already establishes latent/repurposed reasoning directions in base and thinking models; the delta ('steering vectors induced directly in the base model') is a narrow step, and the strong reframing conclusions ('pre-training is when models acquire most of their reasoning mechanisms') go well beyond what the evidence establishes.

strengths: The paper addresses a scientifically important question — whether thinking models acquire new reasoning capabilities or repurpose pre-existing ones — and offers a novel, concrete experimental paradigm (base model as generator, steering vectors as actuators, thinking model as controller) to probe it causally.

The unsupervised SAE-based taxonomy of reasoning mechanisms is a genuine methodological contribution, deliberately restricting latent dimensions to force coarse cognitive categories, with a systematic grid search across layers and cluster sizes (Figure 2) and five different thinking models.

The headline result is strong where it is cleanest: on the Qwen2.5-32B / QwQ-32B pair, the 91% gap recovery on MATH500 was obtained under a narrow default steering setting (Appendix C.3), not the full per-instance sweep, so the flagship claim does not depend on extensive test-time tuning.

Ablation studies (Only-bias, Random-firing, Random-vectors) are well chosen and directly target the alternative explanations that steering is generic biasing or that timing is irrelevant; the finding that category-specific vectors with correct timing outperform all ablations supports the central 'when vs. how' claim.

Reproducibility is strong: code, prompts, hyperparameters, seeds, and one-command reproduction scripts are provided, and limitations (LLM-as-judge validation, weaker results on smaller models) are acknowledged honestly.
weaknesses: Confounding in the hybrid setup weakens the central interpretive claim: the thinking model is deeply embedded in the inference loop (it selects the reasoning category to fire, and its perplexity is used to select which steered token to emit), so the hybrid is not simply 'a base model doing the reasoning.' The paper's framing that base models 'know how' and thinking models only supply 'when' is stronger than the evidence strictly supports.

The evaluation for several configurations involves an oracle-like sweep over steering coefficients and token windows (Tables 4 and 5 show this). Without the sweep, gap recovery collapses (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B on MATH500: 3.5% vs. 56.1%; Qwen2.5-14B on GSM8K: 0.0% vs. 64.7%), indicating the reported gains for smaller/medium models substantially depend on test-time hyperparameter selection rather than a deployable mechanism. The paper buries this in Appendix C.3.

Results are heterogeneous and the headline 'up to 91%' is the best case; one configuration shows negative or zero gap recovery. Generality across model scales is limited, and the paper's broader conclusion about RLVR teaching 'when not how' rests mainly on the largest model pair.

The taxonomy quality metrics (consistency, completeness, independence) are entirely LLM-judge based, with categories generated by o4-mini and evaluated by GPT-4.1-mini; the authors themselves note human validation is lacking. There is circularity risk: the same family of LLMs both defines and grades the categories, and the coherence of 'reasoning mechanisms' as discovered categories is not independently verified.

The steering vectors are trained on thinking-model data and steered at a fixed depth (37%) chosen from prior work on different models; the causal interpretation of what the vectors do (activating 'latent reasoning modes' vs. stylistic/format effects) is argued but not directly demonstrated, e.g., via targeted behavioral analysis beyond aggregate accuracy.
Only two math benchmarks are used for the main causal claim, while the taxonomy is built on MMLU-Pro; the domain breadth supporting the general conclusion about reasoning mechanisms is narrow.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated framework (constructive model diffing) that complements post-hoc model diffing approaches like crosscoders by explicitly reconstructing the base-to-fine-tuned difference and measuring recovery fidelity, rather than only describing representational differences.

The empirical scope is substantial: nine base/thinking model pairs spanning 0.5B to 32B parameters, four RL-trained (Open-Reasoner-Zero), four SFT-distilled (DeepSeek-R1-Distill), and one mixed (QwQ-32B), evaluated on three benchmarks including a held-out Hendrycks-MATH set.

Validation effort is unusually thorough for this area: human validation of every LLM judge (400 annotations, Cohen's kappa = 0.88 for the central benchmark grader; 14/15 category labels matching human annotators), SAE feature-stability analysis across random seeds following the Paulo & Belrose protocol (93.3% matching rate), careful train/test disjointness (MATH500 kept out-of-sample), best-of-three selection via a holdout set that never touches evaluation benchmarks, and four negative-control ablations confirming that each component (category identity, learned vectors, SAE-gated positions) is necessary.

The main finding (RL recovers ~76% of the gap vs. ~11% for SFT-distilled models, with sparse 5-12% token steering ruling out trivial output-biasing explanations) is striking, clearly presented, and connected to intuitive mechanistic accounts (RL optimizes deployment of existing capabilities; SFT imitates a teacher using possibly different mechanisms).
Reproducibility is supported by a public code repository, complete prompts in appendices, detailed hyperparameters, and full published taxonomies for all nine models.

The limitations section is honest and appropriately self-critical, including the acknowledgment that low SFT recovery could reflect either genuine mechanism modification or limitations of the category-vector optimization itself.
weaknesses: The central interpretive claim (RL teaches heuristics while SFT installs new mechanisms) rests partly on a null result (low recovery for SFT pairs) that admits an alternative explanation the authors themselves concede: their category-vector optimization may simply be less effective at capturing SFT-induced changes. The paper argues the gap cannot stem from benchmark performance or taxonomy quality, but this inference is not airtight.

There is a paradigm confound: the RL arm is a single training recipe (Open-Reasoner-Zero) on Qwen2.5 bases whose prompting templates align closely with the steering pipeline, while the SFT arm is essentially one distillation family (R1-Distill) plus one mixed model. With only one recipe per paradigm, 'RL vs. SFT-distillation' generalizations may reflect recipe-specific idiosyncrasies (data, prompt format, teacher model) rather than the training objective per se.

Evaluation asymmetry: thinking models are sampled at temperature 0.6 with 3 rollouts while base and hybrid models decode greedily, so the 'base-to-thinking gap' mixes a training-paradigm difference with a decoding-regime difference; recovery percentages (including values above 100% for ORZ-0.5B) indicate meaningful noise in gap estimation.

Best-of-three selection of category-vector sets by holdout gap recovered, combined with per-category best-epoch checkpointing, introduces selection bias whose magnitude could differ systematically between the RL and SFT arms, potentially inflating the reported recovery contrast.

Taxonomy discovery and most training data are math-centric, limiting external validity of the claim about what training paradigms 'teach' beyond mathematical reasoning; the authors note this but the headline conclusion is stated broadly.

Several taxonomy evaluation metrics (completeness, independence) rely on LLM graders with only moderate human agreement (kappa/r = 0.45-0.52 overall), so the cross-model comparisons of taxonomy quality used to support the 'comparable taxonomy quality' premise are somewhat soft.

Some claims in the 'Sparse interventions suffice' argument are more rhetorical than demonstrated: sparsity of steering does not by itself rule out that the steering vectors encode task-relevant answer information, though the ablations do help mitigate this concern.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated framework ('constructive model diffing') that shifts from post-hoc representation comparison (crosscoders) to explicitly reconstructing the base-to-fine-tuned difference from interpretable components (category vectors + reasoning heuristics), which is a fresh contribution to the model-diffing literature.

The empirical investigation is unusually thorough for this area: nine base/thinking pairs spanning 0.5B-32B parameters, three benchmarks including a held-out set, negative-control ablations (random category, random vectors, magnitude-only, random positions) that properly isolate the contribution of each component, and a sparsity analysis (5-12% of tokens steered) that rules out trivial output-biasing explanations.

Methodological hygiene is above average: LLM judges are validated against human annotators (Cohen's kappa = 0.88 for the scoring judge; 400 annotations), SAE seed-stability is tested following the Paulo & Belrose protocol (93.3% feature matching), and best-of-three selection is done on a holdout mix rather than the evaluation benchmarks, keeping reported numbers out-of-sample.

The central finding (RL-trained models recover ~76% of the gap while SFT-distilled models recover ~11%, with consistent size-matched comparisons at 1.5B and 32B on the same Qwen2.5 bases) is a useful and falsifiable lens on what different training paradigms teach, with practical implications for efficient reasoning-model development.
Reproducibility is addressed via a public codebase, and detailed hyperparameters, prompts, layer choices, and complete taxonomies are provided in extensive appendices.
weaknesses: The headline interpretive claim — that RL 'teaches heuristics over pre-existing mechanisms' while SFT-distillation 'installs new ones' — is a stronger inference than the evidence strictly supports. Low recovery for SFT pairs could equally reflect a failure of the category-vector optimization procedure to capture the SFT-induced changes (which the authors concede in the limitations), rather than genuine mechanism modification. The paper's framing frequently presents the mechanistic interpretation as established when it is one of several consistent explanations.

The RL-vs-SFT comparison is partially confounded: the RL models (ORZ) are trained by one recipe on Qwen bases while the SFT-distilled models come from DeepSeek's pipeline (including a Llama-8B base with a different tokenizer/architecture family). Differences in teacher quality, data, and training scale could contribute to the recovery gap independent of the RL/SFT distinction. The size-matched Qwen comparisons mitigate but do not eliminate this confound.

Some recovery numbers exceed 100% (e.g., ORZ-0.5B at 107.4%) and small SFT pairs show negative recovery, suggesting the hybrid construction can exceed or fall below both endpoints; the gap-recovered metric and its variance properties are not analyzed in depth, and base models decode greedily while thinking models sample 3 rollouts, an asymmetry that complicates strict comparison of accuracies.

Generality is narrow: taxonomy discovery and all evaluation are confined to mathematical reasoning, and the taxonomies themselves are biased toward math-specific features (e.g., 'Arithmetic Computation'), which the authors acknowledge. It remains open whether the RL-vs-SFT conclusion holds for other domains, code, or non-STEM reasoning.

The heuristic extraction depends on disagreement gating between base and thinking model, and category vectors are trained on the thinking model's own next-token signal under teacher forcing; this creates a train/test coupling that inflates the plausibility of the 'mechanisms are pre-existing' story for RL models, and an alternative decoding-mismatch story is not fully excluded.

Taxonomy quality metrics (consistency, completeness, independence) are all LLM-judged with only moderate human-judge agreement on the grading judges themselves (kappa/r = 0.45-0.52 overall), so the claim that 'taxonomies achieve similar quality across model types' — a premise of the central argument — rests on relatively soft ground.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated framework ('constructive model diffing') that complements post-hoc diffing methods (e.g., crosscoders) by explicitly reconstructing the base-to-fine-tuned difference from interpretable components and measuring recovery fidelity.

The central empirical result is striking and interesting: RL-trained models (Open-Reasoner-Zero) recover ~76% of the base-to-thinking gap while SFT-distilled models recover ~11%, suggesting different training paradigms modify models in qualitatively different ways.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for an interpretability paper: nine base/thinking pairs spanning 0.5B–32B, three benchmarks including a held-out set, negative-control ablations (random categories, random vectors, magnitude-only, random positions) that show every component of the construction is necessary, sparsity analysis ruling out trivial output-biasing explanations, and best-of-three vector selection on a holdout mix to keep reported benchmarks out-of-sample.

LLM-as-judge components are validated against human annotators (400 annotations; benchmark judge κ=0.88; 14/15 category labels match human labels), and SAE feature stability across seeds is verified via the Paulo & Belrose protocol (93.3% matching rate).

The paper is honest about limitations (math-biased taxonomies, coefficient-selection confound, the possibility that low SFT recovery reflects optimization limitations rather than genuine mechanism modification) and releases code for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation — 'RL teaches heuristics over pre-existing mechanisms while SFT-distillation installs new ones' — rests on an inference-by-elimination that is not airtight. The key argument ('since both model types reach comparable benchmark performance and similar taxonomy quality, the gap must stem from the category vectors') is a leap: failure of the constructive diff to recover SFT performance could equally reflect limits of the steering/optimization method for those model pairs, which the authors themselves concede in the limitations section. The dichotomy is best read as a hypothesis consistent with the evidence, not established.

The RL vs. SFT comparison is confounded. All four RL pairs use Qwen2.5 bases (the same family the category vectors are optimized in), while the SFT pairs include Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.1-8B bases with different teachers and different training data. The comparison therefore mixes training paradigm with base-family match, teacher quality, and data distribution; the size trend among distilled models (recovery growing with base scale) hints that factors other than paradigm alone are at play.

An alternative explanation for high RL recovery — that RL training moves weights less far from the base model, making the diff easier to capture with a small set of steering vectors — is not clearly distinguished from the 'learned heuristics' narrative; recovery of the diff by the construction does not by itself establish that the thinking model 'uses base-model mechanisms' at deployment.

Some evaluation details introduce noise or asymmetries: recovery percentages above 100% (e.g., 107.4 for ORZ-0.5B) indicate substantial measurement variance on small benchmarks, thinking models are sampled (3 rollouts, temperature 0.6) while base and hybrid models decode greedily, and the 'completeness' metric (LLM confidence in category assignment) is a fairly weak proxy for the claimed taxonomy-completeness property.

The taxonomies are heavily math-biased (acknowledged), limiting the generality of the framework's conclusions beyond mathematical reasoning, and the evaluation pipeline depends on several LLM-based components (o4-mini labeling, GPT-4.1-mini judging, Claude Sonnet grading) whose aggregate error propagation is not fully characterized despite per-component validation.
